doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: How he solos: thinking of nothing, the black space
summary: He explains soloing by absorbing the vibe, comparing it to driving or golf in the zone.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know just to wrap up here, I wondered if you can describe what you think of when you solo. What do you take into consideration?

I’ve done some clinics and I’ve sort of come up with a way, an analogy, at clinics to try and get kids into it. I think of nothing. Absolutely nothing. My best solos are in the black spaces. If you’re going to blow — now this I’m going to say — this isn’t unequivocally correct, this is my view. If you’re going to blow a great solo you can’t have analytical thought get in your way. To me, you already have to know the changes and you already have to know what you’re going to do. You have to allow your ears and your soul to absorb the vibe of the people around you in such a way that you react and they react instantaneous, without thinking. And the only way that happens is when you go into the space and allow yourself to be free inside the space. And so for me I start to blow and all I do is see nothing. I see a black space. And I can see it — I mean you usually close your eyes and see black, but I can see where I go right now. And I can see it’s got a depth to it and I start to blow and I hear what I hear. As a matter of fact I start to blow off what I hear, and if there’s nothing there I still hear that. It becomes a different kind of sound. The space becomes a different kind of sound. For me, that’s the best way to blow. I don’t care what key I’m in, as a matter of fact I don’t want to think about — even on blues, I will not think about the key, because it has no real reason — rather there’s no reason to think about what key I’m in. What am I going to make a mistake? I mean really, give me a break. Everybody makes mistakes. So you don’t care what key you’re in, you don’t care about anything like that, you care only about the space and the validity of the statements you make. It’s like oh try and drive the car — all right you go all the way back to when you first started to drive. You’re taking that first lesson. And they’re telling you okay you’ve got to look in this mirror, you’ve got to look in that mirror, you’ve got to look in this mirror, you’ve got to look behind you, you’ve got to put your seatbelt on, before you put it into gear you’ve got to do this, you’ve got to do that. When you depress the pedal don’t use both feet because if you use this you’ll ride the brake pedal. You have all these rules. Now when you get to the corner look in this direction before you do this and

always look to your left because traffic comes from this direction so you look there first then you look over here. You have all these rules. Try driving the car and thinking about those. You can’t. Try playing golf and trying to think about how you put your hands and what you do and the position of your shoulder and where you — no that’s for when you practice. But when you go to play the game you’re in the zone. When you go to drive the car you’re in the zone. You do it inherently because you’ve practiced enough to do it well. If you do it well great. If you don’t you have an accident. If you don’t you don’t hit the ball right, it slices to the right or it doesn’t do what it’s supposed to do. But when you’re in the zone, when you’re truly doing the job, I’ll defy anyone to say they were thinking about it when they did it. There’s nothing there. It’s the pure thought process. I am right inside and it’s going direct. That’s what I try and get across to the kids when we do clinics. I’m an ear player. I’m a soul player. That’s where I give you what I play. See that’s what makes the difference between somebody that wants me to play on their movie score than somebody else. Because they know what I’m going to give that melody. It’s the name notes in there but they know what I’m going to give it. And that’s the difference. They want what I’m going to give it. So you have — when I’m dealing with the kids — you have that ability to do this. So I make them close their eyes. I just did this at the University of the Pacific last week. The kids wanted to know how to play out. And let me tell you these were not — like these were the cream of the crop from around the country, the University of the Pacific has a really unique program where they bring them in on a scholarship thing from all over the United States into one place and do a week of seminars. Christian McBride was there, Brubeck, ourselves. You do seminars, things, work with the kids and everything, and they put bands together, wonderful program. So these kids, I got a quintet standing in front of me and said, “Play me something.” And they picked a tune, I think it was “Morning Sunrise” or whatever it is.
